meaning:
These lyrics are referring to the consistent loop of the same problems, to the point where it becomes routine.

“And if it’s like that the whole time, we’ll be alright” refers to a false reassurance loop. A point of such a mental draining where a person assumes that if everything is consistently messed up, it’ll be “alright”.

“I stayed up all night, but it’s alright” refers to insomnia becoming part of general routine, where it becomes so normalised to a person, to the point where it isn’t an important issue.

line: Sanity ran and flee like dog, shit is buggin’ me
vault_lines: Sanity ran and flee like dog, shit is buggin' me
meaning:
Could be considered a triple entrendre.

The last part of this lyric can be interpreted as “Dog, shit is buggin' me” as in referring to a close friend as their ‘dog’, and telling them how ‘shit is bugging’. Referring to overall frustration of life.

However, the word usage refers to how dogs can attain flees on their fur, which is often itchy for the dog, causing frustration, which is also expressed using the word “bugging”. This word also refers to how flees are bugs. Where “shit is buggin me” refers to a perspective of a dog dealing with flees. This could be referring to the ‘flees’ being life problems in general, however, there is no way to confirm this.

“Sanity ran and flee like dog” refers to the loss of sanity from the writer, expressing how the sanity of himself is fleeing, similar to a dog running away from home. Where “flee” refers to the act of running away.

vault_lines: Slip a fist up for my niggas in chains, my mental was caged
meaning:
Raising a clench fist has long been a symbol for unity, peace, and brotherhood. It has been used by many campaigns such as the Black Power movement. This is Earl showing his solidarity to inmates who are being held in prison.



Inmates are commonly held in chains, and shackles to restrain them, and also inhibit them from escaping the facility. Earl is comparing his depression, and mental issues to being caged, or locked up in a correctional facility. Although he’s never been to jail he understands the feeling.

meaning:
Earl keeps a close eye on everyone around him, as his paranoid mind doesn’t trust anyone. This was something he expressed in the hook of “Grown Ups”:

Don’t know where I’m going, don’t know where I’ve been
Never trust these hoes, can’t even trust my friends

He figures this close judgement of people he associates himself with and the new way he’s seeing things in general is just something that comes with age.

line: It’s rainin’ a bit I hope it’s a monsoon, my face in the sink
vault_lines: it's rainin' a bit
meaning:
This line expresses how Earl hopes for the worst, even in small setbacks. Though it’s only drizzling outside, he hopes that it escalates to a full-on catastrophic monsoon.



The rain could also be figurative, representing him feeling sad. He hopes to be swallowed by the sadness, creating a monsoon in the process. “My face in the sink” compliments this, showing that he stays inclined to being depressed.

“My face in the sink” could also be in allusion to “Faucet”, the third track from I Don’t Like Shit, I Don’t Go Outside. In the song, Earl touches on his depressive tendencies with a similar metaphor:

The good guy prescribe faith, never caught ‘em
Chasing these rabbits, whole face in a faucet

line: It’s me and my nibblin’ conscience Nigga, I’m fixin’ to give up I’ve been alone for the longest It’s trouble, the way that we joggin’ Nothin’ gon’ save us or stop us Me and my nibbling conscience Nigga, I’m fixin’ to give up I’ve been alone for the longest This spliff, I ain’t splittin’ no time soon My brain split in two,
vault_lines: And if it's like that the whole time
meaning:
His lack of trust in almost anyone combined with his dissociative nature in general has left Earl alone in an ultimate conflict between himself and his depressive thoughts or “nibbling conscience.” He knows that he’s practically “jogging” towards trouble, but can’t help it. All he can do is smoke “spliffs” whenever depression hits, something he mentioned on “Inside” from I Don’t Like Shit, I Don’t Go Outside:

Face-drinking smoker, it help me duck when emotions jab

He feels like he’s about to give into the depression, which is likely an indication of suicidal thoughts. It may also mean he just feels anemic from all the drugs he’s taken and might pass out.

line: Try to make some sense of all this shit in my brain One foot stuck in a tar pit of my ways
vault_lines: Try to make some sense of all this shit in my brain
meaning:
Earl struggles to find logic within his sporadic thoughts. Though he tries to reason with himself, he figures it’s futile since he’s already too deep in his bad habits. He expresses this by playing off the idiom “[to have] one foot in the grave”, saying he has a foot stuck in a tar pit of his ways.

This is similar to the first lines in “Huey”, the opening track from I Don’t Like Shit, I Don’t Go Outside.  However, while the line on “Solace” suggests that his habits are the cause of the problems in question, the line on “Huey” carries connotations that the difficulties he are referencing are not all in his control.

Foot and hand on the gates
We was jumping ‘em, fuck, I’m like quicksand in my ways

This connects to the intro of Part II where Earl convinces himself that he’ll be fine since he’s used to this. Though it may feel worse, he figures this downfall is no different from the depression he’s always had.

Earl is suffering from some sort of crippling depression, and he’s feeling the common symptoms of sedation, devastation, and lack of appetite. To mitigate this, he spends most of his time smoking “spliffs” of weed and feeling weak. In an interview with NPR Music, he elaborated on his eating disorders on tour and how they contributed to his anemia:

I went to eastern Europe. I don’t eat pork, so I wasn’t eating shit ‘cause that’s all they had, and I just… died. I had to cancel tour. And then it wasn’t funny, like, then I was inside. I was fucked up. I was the skinny, like 118. When I was 17, I was 155. […] Over the course of two and a half years, I looked up and I was 118. […] It was too much.

line: But time waits for no man and death waits with cold hands

meaning:
Earl uses the quote “Time [and tide] waits for no man”, which expresses how time will continue to pass no matter the circumstance. He ties this into saying “death waits with cold hands”, showing that death itself is inevitable. He somewhat approached the idea of facing death in “Mantra” from I Don’t Like Shit, I Don’t Go Outside:

You can tell the Reaper I'ma meet ‘em when he send for me
With a cleaver and a .30, and some twisted weed

Basically, Earl is saying that time will continue no matter how depressing or hard life can be and while that time is passing, death is getting closer every second. This can be a good or bad thing depending on how one perceives it.

meaning:
Comedian The Mandal Man provides a tough-love monologue about procrastination as self-avoidance. He flips “waiting” and “chasing” to show they’re the same dodge: stalling for a dramatic external event (“a hurricane”), or sprinting after low-effort dopamine (Uber Eats, club “chasers,” brand-name money “chasing”). The triple pun on chase (pursuit, drink mixers, bank) lands the joke and the indictment. Consumer-app references ground it in modern habits, while the refrain “that’s crazy” undercuts excuses. The fix is agency: get in the gym, pick a hobby, find love, face yourself.

This tongue-in-cheek call to action is a genuine reflection of the album’s big-picture theme: adopt responsibility, continue on the path to maturity, and embody the best version of yourself as an individual.

line: Give my baby my daddy last name and his likeness
vault_lines: Give my baby my daddy last name and his likeness
meaning:
A very profound moment right here.

Earl’s father was Keorapetse Kgositsile, also known as Bra Willie, a renowned South African Poet. Earl has had a very layered and strained relationship with his father as he had been primarily absent throughout his childhood.

Keorapetse was South Africa’s National Poet Laureate and a major figure in anti-apartheid politics. That legacy gave Earl a complicated sense of pride and resentment—he admired his father’s artistry, but resented his absence as described in 2013’s Chum.

However, these lines seem to indicate he has found a new understanding. He has long grappled with his father’s legacy and the things he inherited from him (his writing instincts, “weightiness” and seriousness). In his own way, he is turning his father’s absence into presence.

He often raps about breaking patterns of pain and emotional distance. The idea of him passing down his father’s last name to his newborn baby girl could symbolize his healing as has been a recurring theme throughout this album.

Also worth noting is the duality of “name” and “likeness”. A name is official and institutional. Likeness is physical, spiritual or even genetic. He’s acknowledging both; his dad’s formal legacy and his actual being still live on in him, and will continue to do so now with his child.

vault_lines: Huh, I shot the sheriff, don't expect to get no calls from him
meaning:
Earl references the 1973 reggae classic “I Shot the Sheriff” by The Wailers.

In the original song, the narrator admits to having killed a sheriff who always despised him in self-defense, but he denies the killing of a deputy. Furthermore, he claims the murder of the deputy is being pinned on him to increase the severity of the charges.

According to The Words and Music of Bob Marley, Marley discussed in 1974 how the shooting of the sheriff is a symbol of seeking justice, likely in response to the phenomena of police brutality and disproportionate incarceration of Black people during the 1970s, saying:

I want to say ‘I shot the police’ but the government would have made a fuss so I said ‘I shot the sheriff’ instead… but it’s the same idea: justice.

In a 1975 interview with Karl Dallas for Rock’s Backpages , he presents a more abstract reading of the sheriff in the song, saying:

That message a kind of diplomatic statement…You have to kinda suss things out. I shot the sheriff is like I shot wickedness. That’s not really a sheriff, it’s just the elements of wickedness, you know. How wickedness can happen…But the elements of that song is people been judging you and you can’t stand it no more and you explode, you just explode.

Earl echoes this “explosion” of frustration and anger against wickedness and injustice. However, he expands on the metaphor by warning that the narrator will shoot the deputy as well, and no one will hear of them. The rest of the verse indicates that the narrator is being compelled to act even more violently than previous individuals due to the weight of historical and institutional racism, something he discusses publicly in his music and in a 2019 conversation with his mother at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles, among other places.

Earl raps in the context of stark police violence and brutality and ongoing protests and rebellions in the United States, initially a response to the May 25, 2020 murder of George Floyd by officer Derek Chauvin. The protests eventually included many more names—such as Breonna Taylor, Ahmaud Arbery, and Tony McDade—and a call by activists to either defund or abolish the police.

A June 7, 2020 Facebook post was among one of many claiming that “more than 20 police officers are dead now because of the riots”, a figure potentially based on the FBI’s Law Enforcement Officers Killed and Assaulted (LEOKA) Program. The Officer Down Memorial Page—a nonprofit that honors the lives of local active duty officers—on the other hand, claimed that nine officers had died since the start of the protests. However, only the death of retired St. Louis police captain David Dorn has been linked to the context of violence during protests, according to PolitiFact. That being said, the New York Post claimed that more than 700 law enforcement officers were injured during these protests even though the article does not have a link to the alleged “Justice Department data”. Thus, even in times of heightened tension and conflict with the police, the actual murder of police is rare.

CATCH the VIBE / FETCH the HEARSE

PRESS-in' LINES / LAUren SHIRT

BLESS the GIRTH / WITH IT

The rhyme scheme is:

a_b / d_c
a_c / fg
fg / fg

line: Enemy of the state, fuck a allegation
vault_lines: Enemy of the state, fuck a allegation
meaning:
Earl’s father Keorapetse Kgositsile (A.K.A Bra Willie) was banned from his home country of South Africa in 1961 by the racist Apartheid-era government due to his political writing, and lived in exile for nearly three decades in America and Africa. When Apartheid was ended and the African National Congress gained control, Bra Willie could return to his home country. This separated him and Earl for the vast majority of their lives, and made it so that his father could scarcely recognize his country when he returned.

Earl thus knows that being labeled as an ‘enemy of the state’ is nothing but an allegation that has to do with the authority controlling the country. He has decided he can withstand that: he’ll fight whatever he needs to. The government is like the rain from the previous line; Earl is saying that he will endure through whatever obstacles the crumbling world will try to place in front of him. At some point, the government will change, at some point, the rain will stop too.

line: I had to face what the man in the mirror said
vault_lines: I had to face what the man in the mirror said
meaning:
Note that he’s describing himself as ‘the man in the mirror’. He had been so focused on suppressing his problems that he felt no connection to his own reflection in the looking-glass. He describes his own conscience as some separate entity.

This is where the wordplay comes in: there are two images of manhood that Maxo ‘faces’. One is his own reflection (all of the things he’s been holding back from himself). The other image is the man who told Maxo to ‘never change’. They are being compared to each other– while one man can provide advice and the example of what a man can be, only the “Man in the Mirror” can speak the truth to Maxo about his situation. In other words, this line is the turning point in the story of self-reflection told in this verse. But realizing that he needs to stop lying to himself doesn’t make the task of stopping any easier.

 Realizing all of his pains are his responsibility and that he can’t go back to ignoring his problems, the rest of the verse is much darker and less abstract: he describes the things that drove him to start running from his problems.

line: But he told me, “Never change,” we parted ways (Uh, uh)
vault_lines: But he told me, "Never change," we parted ways (Uh, uh)
meaning:
The older man that Maxo hardly remembers told him to ‘never change’. How is he supposed to go from being a teenager to being an adult if he follows that advice and tries to keep everything the same?

Clearly, Maxo remembered this irony long enough to bring it in for his verse: A man who symbolizes maturity told the immature Maxo to ‘never change’. If he misunderstood the words, it would almost be criticizing him for all of the changes he already made to even get to 23 years of age.

In the U.S, telling someone to ‘never change’ is just a way of telling someone that they shouldn’t change themselves on the basis of peer pressure. Maxo knows what the man meant, but is about to use it for wordplay.

line: Look a man in his face Dreads in the way and on his chains Gold writing in a day, forgot his name
vault_lines: Look a man in his face
meaning:
To explain himself, Maxo takes us into his head. He remembers talking to an older man– his dreads were long enough to get in the way of taking a closer look, long enough even to be on his chains.

This limited description establishes one main thing: this is an older man, the kind of person that Maxo could compare himself against as a youth. Maxo describes this man by his dreads and his chains, both things that are acquired over time (just like maturity). That’s what he remembers, not the man’s name.

He doesn’t remember the name, but he does remember what the man said to him. Why is he referencing this half-forgotten guy on a verse with the world-renowned Earl Sweatshirt? Check the rest of the verse, where Maxo’s ‘vision’ begins to clear up.

line: Growin’ up I know I changed, know that things happen
vault_lines: Growin' up I know I changed, know that things happen
meaning:
The lines here are a good example of Maxo’s focus on perception on ‘WHOLE WORLD’: He knows he’s changed from his past. His 2019 Album ‘Lil Big Man’ was all about that path from childhood to manhood and how being Black in America challenged his vision of that future.

 So if he knows that he’s already been growing up, what’s the deal with the “Devil hittin' my peripherals” line?

One interpretation is that Maxo has accepted that he will change and become a mature person, but he is now realizing he had rushed past his own problems on his way to being a fully mature man. He had a whole album to talk about the struggle, but he’s realizing that it wasn’t enough; he needs to run it back and fix the problems he skipped. The ‘devil’ that he ‘saw’ in ‘his 'peripherals’ is something that he can’t just ignore.

meaning:
Maxo is saying that he’s been chasing success for a while, but has realized he left something behind. He caught the Devil in his ‘peripherals’, on the very edge of missing it.

Notice that his first words are about his chase (‘running after shit’) but he ends up talking about perception and the things he was missing outside of him. Instead of continuing to run, Maxo is going to stop for a second; he needs to take the time to look around for the things he was missing about the world and his self.

You can see this in the words he chooses throughout the rest of this song. Check all of the words that have to do with ‘seeing’, ‘knowing’, ‘looking’. He’s setting up his verse to focus on his perception of now compared to the past.

line: Catacombs, after the glow, the battle carrion Get all that malice out your soul, the efficacy strong I finish what I start, the funeral was hella long I fell asleep, the effigy was short My effervescence lost, but not entirely, I shrug the venom off Kept a tiny piece for times we in a war
vault_lines: Catacombs, after the glow, the battle carrion
meaning:
Similarly to what other artists, such as The Weeknd and Eminem, have done in their songs and video-clips, Earl seems to (metaphorically) “kill” and celebrate the funeral of his past self, in order to move on and change his life.

Since he started his career as an artist at the age of 15, as a member of the hip-hop collective Odd Future (led by his “mentor” and frequent collaborator Tyler, The Creator), Earl has been noticed for his honest, raw and often ultra-violent lyrics, addressing both his controversial relationship with his parents and his heavy struggles with depression, rage and addiction. As a result, throughout the years he has poured out an increasingly harsh response to his psychological crisis in songs from albums such as Doris (2013) and I Don’t Like S**t, I Don’t Go Outside (2015).

However, in 2018, despite suffering multiple personal losses, including his father Keorapetse Kigotsile (sampled by the artist on the commemorative track “Playing Possum”) and his friend and collaborator Mac Miller, Earl seemed to have finally settled differences with his haunted past and finding solace through the recording and the release of the album Some Rap Songs, characterized by experimental instrumentals and lyrics about self-analysis, fame and renewed faith, like on the song “Nowhere2go”:

You went and gave me a cape (Cape)
But that never gave me no hope (Hope, yeah, hope, hope)
I found a new way to cope
It ain’t no slave in my soul
But I keep the memories close by (Close by)
Even when I hit a low (I hit a low)
I still give thanks to the most high

Given the generally introspective atmosphere of “WHOLE WORLD,” Earl is probably remarking his decision to start pursuing a new path of self-improvement, purification and determination.

On a broader metaphorical level, “whippin'” and “paint” may symbolize the act of creating or blending something, beyond drug references. This line could be using wordplay to convey the idea of mixing various elements, similar to the culinary process of creating jambalaya – a dish known for its diverse assortment of ingredients. Earl had many quarrels with his mother when he was younger due to behavioral problems, as he famously spoke on in “Chum” from 2013’s Doris:

Momma often was offering peace offerings

This ultimately culminated with Earl’s mother sending him to Coral Reef Academy, a therapeutic boarding school in Samoa for at-risk boys, in 2010. It can be assumed Earl’s mother also had a problem with Earl’s, at the time, provocative rap career. On “Rusty” from Tyler, The Creator’s 2013 project Wolf, it’s implied by Tyler that Earl’s mother resented him for jumpstarting Earl’s crude rapping career:

Look at that mom who thinks I’m evil, hold that grudge against me
Though I’m the reason that her motherfucking son got to eat

Earl shows maturity here, saying he now knows that his mother was simply worried for his future; she had “visions of sorrow” for him. He persisted with his career after returning from Samoa in 2012 to critical success, but by delving into more grounded, introspective topics in his music. This compromise pleased his mother and allowed him to financially support her by generously “halving” his profit with her, implying that their relationship is repaired.



Earl Sweatshirt and his mother, Dr. Cheryl Harris, at a 2019 interview for the Los Angeles Museum of Contemporary Art.


As a simile to this, Earl refers to a bit from 2007 comedy film Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story where a boy’s body is literally halved.

meaning:
This is played as the last thing in the track before it goes to “Playing Possum”. After all of the things he said about ‘keeping pace’ and wishing peace, he’s recognizing that it isn’t over yet.

If he can’t ‘call it’, it’s not just that he can’t call it quits. Someone’s ‘call’ can mean their decision (“It’s your call”) or their judgement (“I call them like I see them”). He’s unsure about a lot of things, so he has decided to keep trying to support the people around him (to keep pace) while he continues asking questions.

This is something that continues into his future. In the 2020 track WHOLE WORLD, Earl describes the world like this:

I like to think of life as deep, chilly water
We in it, feelin' warm, swimmin' upstream

The world is not warm and hospitable by default. Instead, he comes to embrace the idea that ‘keeping pace’ actually keeps us warm in the cold waters of life. We have to swim against the stream, it’s the only way to stay warm enough to live. He exhorts everyone struggling with him to keep pace, but he cannot make the final call on this as anything other than survival.

For the rest of us, we have to keep up with life– keep our pace.

Earl is right there with us. In his verse, he uses ‘kid’ to punctuate claims. Then in the refrain, he uses ‘dog’, like he’s talking honestly and openly. In this outro, he’s saying ‘my nigga’ because he’s finally talking to somebody and not just bragging or confessing. These last phrases are his honest wish for those who don’t have peace.

line: When it’s time to put my burnt body in a case Tell my momma, I said thank you
vault_lines: When it's time to put my burnt body in a case
meaning:
Earl continues SRS’s focus on familial relationships, confronting perceivably fractured maternal ties with his mother, Cheryl Harris. Earl’s relationship with his mother has often been reflected in pure jest and underlying tension, highlighting a disconnect in their bond. As Odd Future initially emerged in 2010, Earl’s relationship with his mother attracted attention when he was sent to boarding school in Samoa due to poor behaviour. This led to ‘Free Earl’ and ‘Fuck Earl’s Mom’ chants, detailing both the perceivable and tangible breakdown of their relationship. This ultimately harboured a basis of tension which permeated numerous references to his mother in further releases.

Most notably however, this line draws similarities to Earl’s opening verse on the 2015 EP Solace, which was dedicated to his mother;

And when they drag me out the gutter, mail the ashes to my mother”

More recently, Earl’s increasing sense of remorse has conflicted with this enduring tension, exemplifying his discomfort in addressing such nuanced emotions. This is apparent on Knxwledge’s 2016 song “Balance”;

I had to ask moms what I owed to this shit, she said “Nothin'”
She asked me ‘bout them old times both of us miss, I said nothin’
She asked me if I’m smokin' again
I told her that I prolly gotta go in a bit”

Now championing his mother with such reverence represents Earl’s growth and increasing emotional transparency. This further reinforces the album’s thematic emphasis on Earl’s parental relationships. Compounding this reference and following “Veins” is the conciliatory “Playing Possum”, which features Earl’s mother and late father, binding this gesture by accounting for Earl’s parental reconciliation.

line: Damn, they sold me upstream, baby
vault_lines: Damn, they sold me upstream, baby
meaning:
Earl is alluding to the allegory of being “sold up the river”, signifying a deep betrayal. The phrase was originated from slavery the antebellum south of the United States where slaves we’re sold “up the river” deeper in the south where slavery conditions were much harsher, often being separated from family (if not already separated).

https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2014/01/27/265421504/what-does-sold-down-the-river-really-mean-the-answer-isnt-pretty

Earl is likely referring to this as an allegory to signify his perspective during the denouement of the Odd Future era. He may have felt betrayed by his former band-mates, equating the conditions of his obligation to the band with the conditions of slavery.

https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2011/11/river.html#:~:text=In%20reference%20to%20prison%2C%20someone,%2C%20whether%20guilty%20or%20not.%E2%80%9D

The phrase could also be a metaphor for being sent to prison. Either way, the river is a two way stream and either side has some version of slavery or confinement.

 I was terrible. I was awful. For that whole year (…)  I was the worst. I became the one example that people give. (…) After a year, I was the “you don’t want to be like him.”

line: The fare’s high, niggas know they outta wack Sterilize your clique, paralyze maritime niggas when Every time Wavy Don tappin’ in
vault_lines: The fare's high, niggas know they outta wack
meaning:
A fare can refer price you pay to get to a destination using a transportation service. Taking the “n***as know they outta wack” line into account, this could mean that the people Earl was referencing in that line have a long way to go before they’re on his level, or even close to it. They’re “outta wack” because they haven’t completed their journey yet.

Another interpretation could be that because the fare is high, the mentioned people cannot pay to travel any further, therefore they are “outta wack”, stuck in a place where they cannot progress anymore.

As many wipes are used for sterilizing surfaces or other areas, “Sterilizing your clique” could mean “wiping out” the aforementioned clique, either metaphorically or literally.

“Paralyze maritime nas”, tying in with the mention of sterilizing, could mean that Earl is sterilizing your clique, because the clique is composed of “maritime nas”, or fishy folks.
On his 2015 song, “Grief", Earl raps “fishy nas stick to eating off of hooks”. So the “maritime nas“ are just followers, who feed off of what Earl or his peers do. Earl sterilized and paralyzed the clique when he went on a 3 year hiatus without releasing an album, as they had no more of Earl to feed off of.
Maritime is defined by Oxford Languages as “connected with the sea, especially in relation to seafaring commercial or military activity.” The term high fares was used earlier, so when Earl says “the fare’s high”, it is likely that he means traveling by sea, and on his journey he is sterilizing and paralyzing “maritime n***as”.

Finally, “Wavy Don” could possibly be a reference to meteorologist Don Slater, a weatherman on channel WAVY TV 10 for 40 years. So, as Earl is traveling and proving his superiority to others, his mark on the waves and the weather in the sea is so significant that every time Don Slater, the weatherman, taps in, he has a report to make on the change in the weather caused by earl.
“Wavy Don” might be an allusion to Don Roberts, also on the channel WAVY TV 10, who’s been reporting for WAVY for 31 years. Disregarding the sea interpretation, maybe Earl is still paralyzing those followers, and his acts are on WAVY TV 10 news, reported by Don Roberts.

meaning:

Perhaps Earl doesn’t have the best relationship with weed and its sometimes unstable psychoactive effects.

In a 2013 interview with GQ on his life and debut album “Doris” Earl had this to say about his relationship with weed.

line: Jack of all trades, was dealing niggas a handful
vault_lines: Jack of all trades, was dealing niggas a handful
meaning:
The phrase “jack of all trades” is an idiom that applies to an individual who is capable of performing multiple task at the same level of quality. However, it’s important to note that a jack of all trades is not a master in any particular field, but rather just familiar. The phrase is often directed as an insult; emphasizing the lack a person has in mastering any particular skill and is followed up by another phrase, “master of none.”

This line could also be in reference to the playing card “Jack”, which appears in English and French card decks. “Dealing” is a term used in these games to distribute individual cards from a shuffled deck to each player through rotation. Often times, there is typically one dealer that passes the cards to each player. A “hand” is the set of cards that each individual player receives from the dealer.



The 4 different suits of a Jack.





The word handful is also a homonym of “hand full”, which creates even more meaning.

On one hand, Earl Sweatshirt could be using only part of the “jack of all trades” idiom to illustrate his versatility as a rapper compared to his competitors, as opposed to using the phrase literally. Simultaneously, he might also be portraying himself as a dealer distributing hands, meaning he can deal a hand full of support for his comrades or dish out a handful of punishment toward his opposition.

line: It’s real when you seal up letters with wax

New York is also where Earl met the rapper MIKE, who had a hand in creating Earl’s latest project. By summer 2017, he was hanging out at pro skateboarder Sage Elsesser’s place in Brooklyn and listening to music.

His escape to New York reflects the music he makes. His most isolated album, I Don’t Like Shit, I Don’t Go Outside, produced his most depressive songs. Hanging around the members of NYC’s current irregular hip-hop vanguard while making Some Rap Songs seems to have centered him.

It’s crazy… And then from my dad’s poem “Anguish Longer Than Sorrow,” where the last line of that poem is—and I’d say kind of the thesis is—he said, “Let me borrow the rememberer’s voice while I can and say: to have a home is not a favor.” Which just like, for me and people that are in my life, there’s word association with that, and emotion association with that, that’s just like…scratches a good itch.

Ocean also using irony that the show Good Times is playing in the background (and throughout the rest of the song as a white noise effect). You can hear the show’s character Jimmie Walker say his catchphrase, “Dy-No-Miteee!” at 1:05.

“New ice, new glass” also feeds into the drug addiction analogy, as crack and methamphetamine (ice) are often inhaled with a glass pipe. Other possible drug-related double-entendres in the song include “silver spoon” (heroin use) and “bottles of this wine we can’t pronounce” (cough syrup).

He’s drunk, so at this point in the day, each day, he’s only be half-contemplating what jumping and killing himself would do, passing it off as a joke to his friends. It would end the self-destructive cycle he goes through every day.

This also brings the day full circle, as he started the day on the roof and was admiring the view instead of contemplating suicide.

These kids can’t understand the challenges facing people who are less wealthy because they’ve known nothing but luxury. They close their eyes to the needs of the less fortunate, becoming self-centered and taking their enormous wealth for granted.

At the same time, the non-rich are unable to imagine the lives that these kids lead. They can’t understand what the wealthy call “problems.”

Therefore we have to close our eyes to concentrate on the challenges that THEY face, such as a lack of nurturing from would-be authority figures. Another way to think of it is ignoring the current problems by the rich closing their eyes and looking past things they just can’t imagine.

meaning:
The phrase silver spoon means “inherited wealth and accompanying social status.”  Frank, implies ironically in this song that the wealth in his family has negatively influenced him and his life: his parents are busy, he is on drugs. However, as his life flashes before his eyes he realizes how ungrateful he’s been.

The spoon imagery also can be interpreted as representing drug use because some drugs like heroin or crack can be prepared on a spoon. Just two lines later he ‘feels the crash’.

The line can also mean that the rich character’s social status has given him a lot of “food to eat” (things to have), but it hasn’t fed him well, surrounded by countless expensive objects but deprived and malnourished of love and happiness.

“Stories” as in the life stories of Frank, himself, as well as other kids and parents from the upper-middle class whose lives have spun off their desired course.



It also tells us how high he is, compared to the markets (AKA the working class) below. At the end of it all, he ends up dead on the ground next to them, showing that his riches meant literally nothing in his death.

The phrase “The market’s down like 60 stories” primarily serves as an allusive spin on typical statements about economic decline (e.g. “the DOW fell 60 points today”).

This lyric correlates the speaker’s self-destruction with that of a poorly performing “market.” The image evoked in this line and the end of this verse is one of a stockbroker committing suicide after losing his or her shirt in the market.

Through his stint with Odd Future, then even after he was sent to Samoa for boarding school, this problem has always stuck with him. This is very apparent throughout his debut mixtape, EARL, however, it shines the most off of the titular track “Earl”:

Twisted, sicker than mad cattle, in fact I’m off
Six different liquors, with a Prince wig plastered on

Earl would later come back to address his alcoholism later, in the emotionally revealing track “Chum”:

Sixteen, I’m hollow, intolerant, skip shots
I storm that whole bottle, I’ll show you a role model

line: I’m fuckin’ famous if you forgot I’m faithful despite all what’s in my face and my pocket
vault_lines: I'm fuckin' famous if you forgot
meaning:
Through Earl’s success with his Los Angeles based hip-hop collective Odd Future, he has risen exponentially in popularity. This album actually ended up placing at number 5 on the Billboard 200 charts, selling 49,000 copies first week, most likely causing his net worth to jump up as well.

Earl is also pulling off the stereotype that African American males are more likely to cheat than anyone else. According to a survey done by the Institute of Family Studies, men who are married answered yes to cheating 20% of the time, while women were only at 13%. Also coming from the study, the race most likely to cheat is African American, at 22%, while Caucasian is at 16%, and Hispanic at 13%.

Paired with the above stereotype, he also infers that people with a large income will also practice infidelity. Some studies and surveys have suggested that money can make people more likely to do these unforgivable actions. However, despite all of these hypotheticals directed towards him, Earl explains to his significant other that he has remained faithful towards her. He even gives off the sign that he is annoyed that she is even implying this, by the fact he uses a curse word before he explains himself.

Another reason that could be noted as to why Earl has to explain himself as being faithful could be his past. In his previous mixtape EARL, he speaks on themes of sexual assault and speaks of infidelity on multiple occasions, which could lead to this  woman being skeptical.

Frank hints at possible a quadruple entendre with these lines, which can be broken down below:


Frank details how he is on a date with a British girl, with freckles on her face. British people are stereotyped for being very classy, so it can be seen as Frank being with someone out of his league.
Frank has won an International Male Solo Artists ‘Brit Award’ which was designed by artist Damien Hirst, and features polka dots as seen below:






Frank could also be using the word Brit as a homophone for Breit, as in a Breitling watch. The polka dots could be alluding to a diamond bezel.
Frank was born in Long Beach, California and moved to New Orleans at the age of 5. He did multiple odd jobs like: washing cars, mowing lawns, and walking dogs in order to pay for studio time. People who grew up like he did aren’t supposed to be stunting, or doing well for themselves.

This phrase means to steal something, potentially “staining” your criminal record. Earl could be saying that even though he has a rich history of delinquency, he has gotten clean since then, most likely after being sent to Samoa for boarding school. Earl is demonstrating that the money he is making isn’t from criminal activity, it’s from his music.

“Anal” can refer to a type of intercourse, however, in this sense, Frank is using it as being anal-rentative, which basically means fussy or high maintenance. This could possibly be another subtle allusion towards Brown, who during the fight was said to have threatened to shoot Frank.

Earl also means to literally stumble from being intoxicated, tying into the following line.

line: Your hickeys on my aorta and tattoos you could only see
vault_lines: Your hickeys on my aorta and tattoos you could only see
meaning:
The aorta is the main artery of the body, supplying oxygenated blood to the circulatory system, and passes directly over the human heart. Frank is using this statement as a metaphor to how this person has such a deep connection with him. This can also be seen as a bad thing from Frank’s point of view, as this person is metaphorically or emotionally hurting him, leaving their mark on him long after they’ve gone.

As well as the hickeys being a symbol for the physical love, they are also the opposite. To give a hickey, you have to deeply suck on the specific area. Therefore, there’s imagery of this person sucking his heart out, which would tie in with the line’s in the chorus in which both he and Earl say:

All my dreams got more vivid when I stopped smoking pot
Nightmares got more vivid when I stopped smoking pot

“Tattoos you could only see” is simply another sign of his vulnerability to this person, as he is demonstrating how they know everything about him.

line: They thought me soft in high school, thank God I’m jagged Forgot you don’t like it rough, I mean, he called me a faggot I was just callin’ his bluff
vault_lines: They thought me soft in high school, thank God I'm jagged
meaning:
In high school, Frank explains how he wasn’t always the toughest kid, however, in the right situations he could be, thus the use of the word “jagged”.  “Jagged” could also refer to Frank’s sexual orientation, with the idea that he’s not straight. Also, in reference to the last line, “jagged” is the opposite of being straight-edge.

However, the main reason for these lines are most likely shots at Chris Brown. On January 28, 2013, Frank and Chris got into a fight in a parking lot. It was detailed that Brown went to shake Frank’s hand, but when he refused, Brown punched him in the face. It should also be noted, that Frank did say he heard someone yell “faggot” during the scuffle.



It can also be noted that this fight happened on a Sunday, which can be where the name of this track derived from.

A lot of these later shows feature Frank traveling all across the continent, to places like Amsterdam, Copenhagen and Munich. Because of this, it would be understandable that he has jet lag, or flight fatigue, because of all these places he is visiting.

This could possibly be a way to blend the transition into the hook, as Frank is “jet-lagged and restless,” almost as if he is coming down off of marijuana.

line: Give me Bali beach, no molly, please, palm, no marijuana trees
vault_lines: Give me Bali beach, no molly, please, palm, no marijuana trees
meaning:
Molly, also known as MDMA, is a synthetic drug that acts as a stimulant or a hallucinogen. It usually causes distortions in one’s mental ability to perceive reality, as well as distortions in time.

Frank rejects taking these drugs however, in favor of Bali beach, which in particular is significant, since it is an Indonesian island dominated by Hindu temples and religious festivals. This implies Frank wants to reject mind-altering substances in favor of embracing spirituality.



He also calls back to the previous line in which he also rejects marijuana because he dislikes the negatives it causes him to feel.

line: All my dreams got dimmer when I stopped smokin’ pot Nightmares got more vivid when I stopped smokin’ pot
vault_lines: All my dreams got dimmer when I stopped smokin' pot
meaning:
While marijuana has the effects of giving the user a panicked sense in their mind, anxiety and depression, Frank and Earl acknowledge the fact that it can be positive or negative for their creativity as artists. The fact that their dreams are “dimmer” suggests they’ve been brought back to reality, however the night terrors may show the bad side.

In a more literal aspect, smoking pot before sleeping makes recalling dreams difficult, and those who smoke pot everyday may experience REM-rebound when they stop, meaning their dreams or nightmares for a couple of days are more vivid and easily recalled. Also, frequent night-terrors are a common side-effect of quitting marijuana.

In an interview with Pitchfork promoting the release of Doris, Earl commented on the hook of this song:


Pitchfork: The hook on “Sunday” mentions that you stopped smoking weed. How long did you go without?

Earl: A long-ass time, when I got pneumonia. I kind of just started smoking weed again.

Earl also alters the popular phrase “to wear your heart on your sleeve,” which means to make one’s emotions visible and vulnerable, to instead shelving his emotions on the “top cupboard.” This is symbolic of Earl’s destructive state that he has been in throughout this mixtape, as he is primarily blaming his father for his actions. line: Signal’s weak, sleep in Faraday Cage
vault_lines: Signal’s weak, sleep in Faraday Cage
meaning:
A Faraday cage is a device to block electromagnetic radiation that ordinarily can penetrate structures. Conductive material in a lattice pattern will block EM waves at a frequency determined by the size of the lattice. While Faraday cages often are built intentionally to prevent electromagnetic interference with electronic equipment contained within them (or to prevent equipment that emits EM waves from interfering with other systems), they can be unintentional: buildings and houses covered in stucco often have notably poor mobile phone reception due to the hexagonal steel lath that forms a matrix to which the wet stucco binds as it dries.

Individuals who believe themselves to be sensitive to even trace amounts of electromagnetic radiation (a view generally dismissed by conventional medicine as quackery since the 1990s) often construct an additional Faraday cage for their sleeping area, in the belief that the electromagnetic fields generated by ambient radio waves and even the alternating current running through the wires in their walls can harm them.

The NFL’s Houston Oilers then signed him in 1984, and he was the perfect fit for the pass-happy “run and shoot” offense implemented by swashbuckling head coach Jerry Glanville the following year. While he never enjoyed much postseason success, Moon’s howitzer arm threw many long touchdown passes; he held numerous NFL passing records at the time of his retirement in 2000. Moon was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2006.

Some deft wordplay and layered imagery from Moor Mother here.

“Sky walker” is a reference to the Skywalker family of the Star Wars saga. “Nina” here is almost certainly Nina Simone, the legendary singer, songwriter, pianist, and icon of Black femininity.

“Nina in the jungle with diamonds” is a play on “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds,” John Lennon’s universally known psychedelic pop song from the Beatles‘ 1967 magnum opus Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band. The first stanza of “Lucy…” begins, “Picture yourself in a boat on a river,” the principal setting of Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness, which takes place in the Congo Free State during its time as a personal possession of King Leopold of Belgium–as referenced in the next line. Marlow, the protagonist of Heart of Darkness, sees the dark-skinned Black natives of Congo in an essentially psychedelic way, as white flashes of eyes and teeth through the trees. Nina Simone herself had notably dark skin, which meant that she too would have been invisible to Marlow.

line: Get the fuck back, you moving like they cut your ’caine, ayy
vault_lines: Get the fuck back, you moving like they cut your 'caine, ayy
meaning:
Earl is comparing his mental struggles to those experienced during one or more difficult situations. The ambiguity mainly stems from the word “cut,” which can be understood to mean “to take away” or “to reduce the purity of.”

The first potential meaning is referencing the widespread phenomenon of cutting cocaine with other substances, especially the opioid fentanyl, in the United States. Fentanyl and other substances used to cut cocaine are extremely dangerous and even small amounts can result in death. Because of its potency, fentanyl is a major factor in the U.S.’s opioid epidemic, which was a major issue when Earl was producing the album. In addition, Mac Miller, who was close friends with Earl, died after consumption of cocaine, fentanyl, and alcohol two months before the release of Some Rap Songs. According to investigators, the cocaine he was taking was likely cut with fentanyl, which led directly to his death.



Another possibility is that Earl means that he’s moving like someone took away his cocaine, leading to withdrawal. Cocaine withdrawal can cause symptoms such as difficulty concentrating, slowed thinking, exhaustion, restlessness, inability to feel pleasure, depression, and anxiety, all of which can be felt in this song and throughout the album.

Whether Earl is referencing the removal or impurities of cocaine, he is certainly making a play on words with “cut your ‘caine” and “cut your cane.” In this instance, “cane” refers to the walking aid used for the injured and elderly. If someone cut his cane, he would be hobbling unevenly, as the length would not support him in a normal walking motion.

Earl Sweatshirt is referencing two aspects of South Africa’s history:


“Port Wine” references South Africa’s expansive wine industry, specifically Cape Port Style Wine.  This reference also ties back to previous mentions of Earl’s alcohol and drug addiction, as well as the motif of red liquid (blood) running throughout the album. The South African wine industry was only able to grow into what it is through the blood of Apartheid and discrimination, which ties into the next aspect of South Africa’s history.
“Pages of Pass” references the South African Pass Laws, a series of laws that segregated and restricted the movement of black Africans, who were forced to carry passports at all times.  These laws were strengthened during the beginning of Apartheid, and were repealed in 1986.



Earl Sweatshirt’s father, Keorapetse Kgositsile, was a South African poet and activist, who died in January 2018, a little under a year prior to Some Rap Songs' release.

line: They start hackin’ when they can’t shrink us
vault_lines: They start hackin' when they can't shrink us
meaning:
The words “hack” and “shrink” both have double meanings here.

First, “hacking” refers to chopping at something with an axe, while to “shrink” something is to make it smaller. This could refer to workers' rights movements (as referenced a few lines ago), that when companies or the government cannot shrink the numbers of workers on strike they will resort to more violent means (hacking).

Second, “shrink” is another word for a psychologist or psychiatrist, and a “hack” is someone who is incompetent at their job. So, Earl could be saying that when a shrink fails to properly diagnose him or help him with his problems, they resort to using the methods of a hack, either misdiagnosing him or prescribing him something they should not have.

Both interpretations create a vision of an authority figure failing to do something by professional, legitimate means, and resorting to less respected methods toward the end that they seek.

line: Blinkin’ for some feasible methods to free yourself Split it with my hand like cigarill’s Slick oil in a fish’ gill
vault_lines: Blinkin' for some feasible mеthods to free yourself
meaning:
Earl describes one of the ways that help him free himself from isolation: smoking marijuana, one of the few habits left of the series of addictions that once marred his physical and mental health. The rapper has frequently addressed his mixed relationship with weed throughout the years, with a notable example being found on his 2018 song “The Mint:”

Know I use too much of everything at hand
Except the difference is now I control it, I be
In the crib and in the moment, stuck sippin' out the flask
Feet up on the dash, I hit the spliff but don’t promote it

Specifically, Earl refers to the technique used to turn store-bought cigarillos in wraps for blunts, as the tobacco leaves of the cigar are typically split open by hand, filled with cannabis, and then smoked.

While using drugs give the artist a momentary sense of escape, he also illustrates, through a fish-related metaphor, how doing so is ultimately unhealthy, and how he needs something different to find real relief again. A 2017 study proved that fish who exposed to crude oil instead of being immersed in water become slow to respond to predators, and therefore way more vulnerable.

Earl previously used fish-related metaphors on tracks like “Grief” (2015), where he talked about mediocre rappers getting exploited by major labels, and “MTMB” (2019), where he paid tribute to his late father, poet Keorapetse Kgositsile.

While it could be read literally as “noose,” Earl’s word choice here also aligns with the concept of the noûs in ancient Greek and Eastern Orthodox thought — the “spiritual eye” or highest faculty of the mind, able to perceive divine truth.

Saying “my noûs is golden” frames the line as Earl claiming clarity, wisdom, and vision refined through struggle — his insight is not just sharp, it’s precious.

line: Somebody tooted in the student commons The bell rang He went home then argued in the comments

meaning: At surface level, Earl is simply saying that someone farted (“tooted”) in the student commons (presumably some common space in a college?) and then went home and argued in the comments of a social media post, maybe due to some embarrassment or feelings of insecurity. Quite the funny bar. However, when you put the words “tooted” and “common” together, it sounds phonetically like “Tutankhamun”, which is the name of one of the last pharoahs of the eighteenth dynasty of the middle kingdom. Tutankhamun is sometimes known as “the boy king” in popular culture and by egyptologists, as it is believed he became pharoah at about 8 or 9 and ruled until his death at about 18 or 19 (which, curiously enough, is the age of freshman level college students.) Though there is some debate as to what the meaning and origin of Tutankhamun’s name is, it is generally believed to mean “living image of Amun” in ancient egyptian. Amun is the egyptian god often thought of as the leader of the pantheon, and is also known as Amun-Ra, or simply Ra. And what was the ancient egyptian city in which Ra had the most worship devoted to him? Thebes. Earl Sweatshirt’s name is Thebe Kgositsile.

line: Throwin’ up a prayer, it’s a Hail Mary (Woah, where it’s at?)
vault_lines: Throwin' up a prayer, it's a Hail Mary (Woah, where it's at?)
meaning:
A double entendre regarding “Hail Mary”:

Although he’s “never been religious” as he says in the next line, Mac is desperate for some serenity and peace of mind—so desperate that he has resorted to praying. He compares this last resort attempt at prayer to throwing a “Hail Mary”, a football play where all of the receivers run straight for the end-zone and the quarterback throws the ball as far as he can, “praying” for it to be caught. It’s typically reserved for the last play of the game as a desperate attempt to score when you’re losing and have exhausted every other option. It is often a rare chance of success, but the reward is immense if it works.



The “Hail Mary” throw ultimately gets its name from the traditional catholic prayer that addresses Mary, the virgin mother of Jesus. This prayer is known as the Hail Mary, or the Ave Maria in Latin, which is also the title of another Mac song from Faces. The full prayer reads:

Hail Mary, full of grace,
The Lord is with thee.
Blessed art thou amongst women,
And blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.
Holy Mary, Mother of God,
Pray for us sinners,
Now and at the hour of our death. Amen.

Mac could be saying that he is “throwing up” this specific prayer to the Heavens, much like a quarterback would “throw up” a Hail Mary pass.



Note that this is one of the last lines of his verse – as in, he’s tried everything to escape his demons and find peace of mind / save himself and nothing has worked. The only move he has left is to throw up a prayer, a long shot, in the hopes that it might save him. Hence the reason the next few lines are about religion, spirituality, and potentially taking his last breath.

line: I thought I saw a fountain
vault_lines: I thought I saw a fountain
meaning:
PROPOSED SUGGESTION:

I think that this line might be an allusion to Vladimir Nabokov’s ‘Pale Fire’. In the novel, a poet named John Shade envisions a white fountain while he is on the verge of death. He later reads about a woman who had a similar experience. Shade thus believes that this white fountain is a universal symbol that explains or represents what is beyond death.

Shade later learns that the woman had not seen a fountain but rather a mountain; there was a printing error in the magazine that he had read. Shade had conjured up this image of a white fountain and had imbued it with universal meaning, only to learn that its significance arose out of coincidence. As such, the poet had experienced a mirage in a way, believing a vision to be representative of something greater when it was not.

Earl Sweatshirt, then, might be saying that he has undergone something similar to Shade, having thought that he had come to understand some grand truth about our existence only to learn that it was all a misunderstanding. Alternatively, Sweatshirt might just simply be saying that he saw a mirage.

line: Fixed a plate of eggs and bacon, glass of OJ Simpson

OJ can stand for “orange juice,” or can be alluding to famed running back Orenthal James Simpson, or O.J. Simpson. O.J. played for the Buffalo Bills and the San Francisco 49ers during his career, where he led the league in rushing yards for multiple years, which earned him the nickname “The Juice.”

On June 12, 1994 Simpson’s ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were brutally murdered outside of her home, wherein O.J. became a prime suspect. The proceeding trial eventually got dubbed the, ‘Trial of the Century,’ as Simpson pleaded not guilty and hired a team of prominent lawyers such as Johnnie Cochran to defend his case. He was eventually acquitted in this case.



O.J. eventually got arrested again, charged for robbery in Las Vegas in 2007. A jury found him guilty on all charged and he was sentenced to prison, but was granted parole in 2017.

This also provides foreshadowing into the remainder of the song, as Earl eventually murders the girl he is stalking. It should also be noted that with this mention of O.J., the track’s very peaceful beginning gets abruptly ended, and the violence and aggression Earl has showed on the previous tracks start to come back.

Two months after this song released, in May 2010, Earl and Tyler, the Creator released a song entitled “Orange Juice” as well.

“Gleaning what I can from what I have amassed”

Gleaning = carefully picking out useful bits.

Suggests reflecting on one’s past experiences, knowledge, or achievements, and taking lessons from them.

“The space-time continuum bend, I’m sticking with the simple plans”

“Space-time continuum bend” = something vast, cosmic, complicated, maybe overwhelming. Could also mean how unpredictable or surreal life feels.

“Sticking with the simple plans” = choosing to stay grounded, humble, not getting lost in the complexity.

“I’m just a man”

A reminder of humility and limitation.

Despite big ideas (cosmic imagery, achievements, lessons), Earl grounds himself in humanity.

line: Flirts with danger, we hastily learn how to dance

“Flirts with danger”

Suggests playing with risk, being drawn to thrilling or risky situations.

“Flirt” implies not full commitment, but teasing/enticing, like someone testing the edge.

“we hastily learn how to dance”

“Dance” here isn’t literal—it’s symbolic of adapting, moving skillfully, or finding rhythm in chaos.

“Hastily” means quickly, without much time to prepare.

Putting this meaning together, Earl plays with risk then quickly learns how to adapt gracefully to the danger.

The term is used as the title for the album.



Bars of soap are often placed on the rims of bathtubs, so Earl uses a double entendre to describe his lyrics as cleansing and therapeutic.

Interestingly, Earl performed this song back in June 25, 2023 at the Outbreak Festival in Manchester, so him mentioning the album title references how old this album truly is. Live dates back to 2022, during the NBA Leather Tour.

line: The wick out, it’s still really lit They gather around when they hear the cl— They gather around when they hear the click My back to the crowd, a man on a mission
vault_lines: The wick out, it's still really lit
meaning:
Lyrics are “they gather around when they hear the click”

Earl gives us a triple entendre here.

The first layer is a weed bar in the sense that he’s about to light a joint/spliff and everyone around him has a Pavlovian response to the sound of a lighter.

The second is he’s such an amazing rapper that whenever he steps in the booth, a crowd forms around him. The click in this context is a backing metronome, which is often called a ‘click track’ in audio engineering.

The final meaning is him shouting out his crew or “clique” of underground rappers such as MIKE, who handles the first half of this shared project, and Niontay who also features on an earlier track. Earl is saying they attract attention whenever they are together. This is reinforced in the final line as Earl often raps towards his friends with his back to the crowd when he’s performing.

The final line is also a reference to how Earl’s career has been spent going off the beaten path and moving in unexpected directions  (such as releasing a trap album, for example).

‘He could also be carrying it to honour those wrongfully imprisoned resultants of laws now annulled, most of said persons being African-American and in possession of miniscule amounts of weed. line: Everything you utter doesn’t escape, running man
vault_lines: Everything you utter doesn't escape, running man
meaning:
Following the Funny Games reference with another allusion to an unsettling psychological thriller in Stephen King’s ‘The  Running Man’ — a novel in which a man living in a dystopian America participates in a gameshow where he must escape a squad of hitmen for 30 days.

Several aspects of the story can be applied to Earl here; including the protagonist’s attempts to reveal truths about the state of the world hidden in messages and ensuing struggles with censorship.

More directly to the line, I interpret it as an followup by Earl on his assertion about how ‘stakes plummet when you play funny games’ in that Earl’s now adding that these people can’t talk their way out of it with “anything they utter” — he sees through them and they can’t escape.

I’m confident that themes of The Running Man play heavily into this song as Earl has already referenced that he’d “rain flames” and the novel famously ends with the a plane crash and the description “The explosion was tremendous, lighting up the night like the wrath of God, and it rained fire twenty blocks away.”

Worthing nothing is that Stephen King originally released The Running Man under a pseudonym to “ensure people actually liked his work” which is a concept Earl assumedly appreciates or relates to.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Basically, accountability will catch up.

Learning to swim in a pool where a boy drowned last year matches Billy Wood’s motif in the previous verse about surviving, at all costs and against adversity.

With Wax in his ear, E L U C I D could avoid death’s temptation in the water. The voices he couldn’t make out clearly were tempting him, or were they the voices of those who’ve passed, tying in with Earl’s intro regarding his father’s body “swollen behind [his] eyes”.

This also fits in with Earl’s theme in the previous verse about always moving forward and thriving by just living life and appreciating the small moments, something that is supported by the montage of small snippets of life Billy Woods presents throughout this verse.

line: The heavy measure did ’em in The message couldn’t be missed The head was on a stick where it belonged My February never ends
vault_lines: The heavy measure did 'em in
meaning: The chorus begins with, “The heavy measure did ‘em in / The message couldn’t be missed.” The phrase “heavy measure” evokes imagery of forging metal, connecting to the song’s title and the thematic ideas of creation, heat, and pressure. It also works as a metaphor for harsh realities or consequences that cannot be ignored, with “did 'em in” suggesting defeat or being overwhelmed. The next line, “The head was on a stick where it belonged,” continues this imagery of judgment and consequence, possibly symbolizing those unable to withstand the pressure or trials of life. “My February never ends, it isn’t long” references Earl’s birthday on February 24 and his Pisces identity, framing February as a period of purification, introspection, or emotional processing that continues for him even when it ends for others. It can also be read as commentary on ego or the personal cycles of self-examination that define his artistry.

February 24th is Earls birthday. February is associated with purification, the spiritual passing of Aquarius’s winds being left behind leaving only the water making way for Pisces. line: I’m on my off-foot again, I pick apart the defense with the triple-cross Silver hearts, a spliff for your scars Jog my memory, what isn’t ours? Slivers of God ad infinitum
vault_lines: Slivers of God ad infinitum
meaning:
Having his plan thrown off, he has to break down the new adversity in his path. His main goal is to hold high faiths through this and remain loving, lighting a spliff to laugh through the scars with silver hearts in mind that symbolize the protection found in that love and faith, and continuing an inner monologue he started on Azucar, “What’s mine, what good is it if it’s not,” he reminds himself of the sentiment he shared on Lye, and shifts the contextual focus from what doesn’t belong to everybody to what’s capable of being possessed by everyone. That being faith in the only infinite source.
The triple cross represents Jesus and the two thieves, so to break down the defense using the triple cross means to use the understanding of the choice of faith as a means. This turns this passage into a resource for interpreting the rest of the verse.

Earl also could be using a semantic field associated with soccer. “On my off-foot” refers to a player using their non-dominant foot to kick the ball, and to “pick apart the defence” would refer to an attacking player getting past the opposing team’s defences on the pitch. Finally, a “triple-cross” likely refers to a type of pass known as a “cross”, where the ball travels across wide areas of pitch in the air to reach the center of the pitch, and closer to the goal. A “triple-cross” could refer to three crosses by three players being chained together.

line: Tunnel vision, stuck like barnacles on what’s propping the big picture up Stick along for the ride long enough We ending up fine for once, finally, fuck
vault_lines: Tunnel vision, stuck like barnacles on what's propping the big picture up
meaning:
The “what” that is propping the big picture up is a metaphor for the ontological framework that enables reality. He is lamenting time spent navigating the fundamental minutiae of life, and allowing relief after coming to familiarise himself with purposeful being.

This feels like a nod to Plato’s allegory of the cave where the truth is mistakenly assigned to shadows, and a macroscopic lens allows an enlightened perspective to see the shadow is being caused. Similarly, it feels like Earl is orienting himself towards truth, and resents time spent gravitating towards other directions.

line: Acting staticky as if he needed some buzz
vault_lines: Acting staticky as if he needed some buzz
meaning: “Staticky” here refers to feeling tense, jittery, or ‘charged,’ like someone whose energy is haywire. “Buzz” works as both nicotine stimulation and a literal low electrical hum. Earl links the two because they sit in the same conceptual space in their literal senses, unstable electrical energy (“static”) versus activated stimulation (“buzz”). The way they’re used in the lyric suggests a transition from restless energy (“staticky”) to a desired state of stimulation or relief (“buzz”), tying together the literal electrical imagery and informal slang imagery into one overarching idea. This technique is known as cross-domain semantic imagery.

line: If we join the second line The ancestors’ll hand us a drum to load the second time
vault_lines: If we join the second line
meaning:
The “second line” is a tradition of revelry at parades brought to Louisiana by enslaved Africans. The second line would consist of a crowd of musicians and dancers that marched behind the main parade playing energetic rhythms. Second lines brought extra life to parades that were more somber – such as funeral processions – and were seen as an expression of individual freedom in the immediate aftermath of emancipation. The fact that he’s given a “drum to load” implies filling up the clip of a gun, which nods to the subversive nature of second lines during the Jim Crow era.

Interestingly enough, one could also take this as an allusion to loading up a drum track. Second lines usually involved younger adults playing drums while adults danced in the parade; Mavi’s father was a music producer and exposed him to many of his musical influences as he explains in this interview.

In moments of darkness where gratitude is far away, he feels cursed and fated to experience life in this way – but how can you escape fate?

As mentioned earlier in the verse, these lumps and bruises are channeled into his craft. “Grooves”, while recalling scars here, also literally refer to his songs. The term “groovy” comes both from the rhythm of a song and the literal grooves in a record, calling back to the turntable imagery used in the verse.

Earl is alluding to the fact he wants to be the best in the game, and his drive to do so is unparalleled. His past 3 albums have all been critically acclaimed, growing his fame exponentially, especially with the release of his last album in November 2018, Some Rap Songs. This line could also be referencing a bull and a matador. Bulls are color-blind to red so they are likely irritated not by the color, but by the cape’s movement as the matador whips it around. This could symbolize a misunderstanding in Earl’s music. It should also be noted that the name “EL TORO” translates to “THE BULL”.

This could also be calling out some fans who don’t like the change in subject matter from his past album, and want Earl to put out a project similar to Doris. This could also be an allusion to the Red Sea, a body of water inlet of the Indian Ocean and extremely salty. It can be noted that seasoned salt is also red.

In a 2018 interview with NPR, Earl was asked how he felt about finally being able to be himself and not thinking about what others want him to be, he responded with:

…[I’m] such a wildly different person. Not having my identity stamped out for myself early on really had me like on some tofu s***, like just taking on the flavor of whatever

line: I keep my sentences short

Tracks such as “Oldie” are very credible proof of Earl’s unparalleled ability to use wordplay, complex diction, and general grammar tweaks to string together lengthy technical rhyme patterns, often rhyming as many internal multi-syllable sentences with each other as possible. But as Earl’s lyricism has advanced over the years, he has chosen to depart from such lyricism, and instead chosen to shift focus to more concise bars that have far more emotional density, sincerity, and atmosphere to favor reliability and personality over technical skill.

The first song that makes reference to this progression of style is in the song Nowhere2go, which marked the first single released since his departure from the old style. In the song he says:

Tryna refine this shit, I redefined myself
First I had to find it (Uh)"

As American author Ernest Hemingway once replied to the author William Faulkner when he said Hemingway had “no courage,” as he chose to use less ‘complex’ words in his work. Hemingway responded, “Poor Faulkner. Does he really think big emotions come from big words? He thinks I don’t know the ten-dollar words. I know them all right. But there are older and simpler and better words, and those are the ones I use.”

This idea of making things short and simpler has become predominate in this era of Earl in many ways. How most of his songs from both Some Rap Songs, and Feet of Clay, only average up to around two minutes in length, as well as his reasoning for titling his previous album ‘Some Rap Songs’, as it is concise and simple.

line: Intro
vault_lines: I'm as stiff as rock man. Come along the—
meaning:
Not one hundred per cent sure, but I wonder if this song deals in part with Earl feeling pressured by his fanbase?

The whole track sees Earl refer to himself in third person as “the boy”, from someone else’s perspective, and opens with a bar about him having “been gone a few summers too long”. So maybe that’s fans getting impatient, waiting for a new project?
Then, the first half of the verse seems to give an image of Earl smoking weed with a bunch of people who come into his house (“Niggas come in the door and smoke somethin'”). He then faints (“his head thump on the floor”) and the people in his house “press up on” him, refusing to accept any more “bluffin'”. Maybe that refers to Earl’s fanbase refusing to take anymore bluffing on his part about his plans to make a new album?
In that case, the image of Earl fainting maybe gets across his belief that his fanbase – or just the people around him generally – don’t understand how much pain he’s in. They chase after him for more music, and he’s feeling a lot of pressure from it – “I’m just makin' sure my promise is kept.”

I say this partly because I remember, when Earl revealed on Instagram that his father had died, that a lot of fans were commenting asking when the new album was coming out. Maybe Earl has had similarly unpleasant interactions with fans before?

Earl is encouraging the listener to go out in style. To ‘chuck a deuce’ is to hold your index and middle finger up as a way of saying hello or goodbye. It symbolizes the use of the word ‘peace’ as a way of greeting or expressing farewell to someone. Earl is saying that if you know it’s the end, be classy about it and throw up a farewell for everyone.

This symbolizes the fact that Earl has been thinking about death so intensely for so long, that the idea is no longer scary. Earl finds it appropriate to just throw up a peace sign and go out classy, representing how far gone he has become in his worsening depression.

line: Pendulum swinging slow A degenerate moving
vault_lines: Something sinister to it,
meaning:
It’s some very clever nerdplay. In physics, a pendulum’s motion is said to be “degenerate” as friction increasingly slows it down. However, the word “degenerate” can also mean an immoral or corrupt person. Earl is describing the pendulum’s motion as well as saying he is a moral/corrupt person who is becoming more corrupted with time.
Rolling on, “pendulum swinging slow” is a twist on “chain swinging low” lines that’s common in rap. A pendulum looks a lot like the medallions found on the end of chains. I also think Earl isn’t a fan of ‘bling bling’ rap lines, which would be why he wants to play off those lines with a possible Poe reference, giving some depth to an otherwise shallow idea.

#POE REFERENCE?

This could possibly be a reference to Edgar Allan Poe’s short story “The Pit and the Pendulum.”. In the story, a prisoner wakes up to find himself strapped to a wooden board by ropes. When he looks up, he sees a gigantic pendulum swinging slowly back and forth. To his horror, it is also slowly sliding downwards. As the pendulum reaches a point inches above his heart, he is able to break free of the ropes

The Poe interpretation is very interesting. However, it only works if we consider the completion of the line to be “a degenerate moving.” The first suggestion seems more accurate as he continues with “a degenerate moving through the city with criminal stealth.”  Most importantly, there is no mention of the pendulum bearing a scythe like the one found in Poe’s story.

line: [Intro: Vince Staples & Earl Sweatshirt] “What’s up, nigga? Why you so depressed and sad all the time like a little bitch? What’s the problem, man? Niggas want to hear you rap. Don’t nobody care about how you feel, we want- we want raps, nigga.” “Raps?”
vault_lines: In the midst of a tornado, misfitted, I'm Clark Gable
meaning:
Vince Staples is a friend and close collaborator of Odd Future. In this intro, Vince is telling Earl to lighten up and rap (mocking many of Earl’s fans and critics who have the same mindset), and to stop being so depressed about things going on his life (e.g. his grandmother’s death, his struggle with addiction, being sent to Samoa for a couple years)

The introspective nature of a lot of Earl’s songs are often taken at face value, being viewed as mere lyrical exhibition. Vince’s parody highlights that there’s personal struggle to get out of the lyrics themselves. Earl is deeply troubled about things like his grandmothers death and feels like fans don’t understand, which in turn makes him feel like he is being used.

This may also be a callback to “Thisniggaugly,” on Earl’s self-titled debut mixtape EARL, where Tyler and Taco pressured Earl to “say something,” or rap.

Stay off the block, niggas

line: Stuntin’ these niggas gon’ flop like Divac
vault_lines: Stuntin' these niggas gon' flop like Divac
meaning:
Flopping is a term from basketball, it is an intentional fall by a player after little or no physical contact by an opposing player in order to draw a personal foul. This type of action is known as being unsportsmanlike.

Further, Vlade Divac is a Serbian-American professional basketball player who has played for multiple teams in the NBA, but has spent the most at the Los Angeles Lakers, the city where Earl resides. Divac has earned a reputation as a flopper, often found at, or near the top of lists ranking the greatest floppers in NBA history.



Thus, here, Earl is saying that when he shows off his skills, others have to resort to unsportsmanlike conduct to try stopping him–this also makes the statement that he can’t be beaten fairly. More notable, other rappers can “flop” when it comes to album sales or plays, which basically means they do poorly.

Nah, no, nah, nah, fuck that. Niggas think ‘cause you fucking made 'Chum’ and got all personal that niggas won’t go back to that old fucking 2010 shit.

meaning:
Despite the growth of Earl’s success and maturity since being sent to Samoa in 2009, it would appear that there is still a considerable disconnect between Earl and his mother.

Earl feels remorse for his younger self’s behaviour and demonstrates a sense of responsibility and concern for his mother, offering to reimburse her (monetarily, or perhaps with time and effort) for what he believes he deprived her of in his earlier years.

Earl’s mother tells him that he owes her nothing, before asking about Earl’s past and their history together, perhaps in a desperate attempt to reawaken the maternal bond. Her son does not reply.

Motherly instincts kicking in, Earl’s mom begins to fuss over him, a sign of parental affection that is often misunderstood or taken for granted. She is concerned that Earl is smoking weed again – presumably a topic of some tension between the two. Unfortunately, Earl still feels too awkward, disjointed and uncomfortable in this situation to open up to his mother, prompting him to express a desire to leave – terminating yet another strained encounter with the parent that raised him.

Mark 14:22-24 describes The Last Supper:

And as they did eat, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and brake it, and gave to them, and said, Take, eat: this is my body.
And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank of it.
And he said unto them, This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many.
Verily I say unto you, I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine, until that day that I drink it new in the kingdom of God.

‘Teddy Kollek in his memoirs wrote that it was necessary to knock down the quarter because a pilgrimage to the wall was being organized with hundreds of thousands of Jews, and their passage through the “dangerous narrow alleys” of the “slum hovels” was unthinkable.’
