‘Twenty-odd Jerusalem building contractors, hired by Kollek, first knocked down a public lavatory with sledgehammers. Army bulldozers were then brought in to raze the houses.’

‘The residents were given either a few minutes or fifteen minutes to evacuate their homes. They initially refused to budge. In the face of this reluctance, lieutenant Colonel Ya'akov Salman, the deputy military governor, issued an order to an Engineering Corps officer to start bulldozing.’

‘An interview given two decades later by Eitan Ben-Moshe, the engineer attached to the 'IDF’ Central Command who oversaw the operation, she was not the only victim. Earl cleverly flips this by saying he asked Jesus' “baba”, which is a common word amongst various South African languages meaning “father”, to cast the stone at him, as he is stating that only God can judge him and keeping this faith despite what appeared to be unanswered prayers, as he begins the line with “Answer me please”.

line: Gotta keep it brief, the liturgy, it had to be poems

meaning:
Poetry is often utilized as a way to condense the human experience into its core components. Short stanzas and verses can encapsulate entire lifetimes of experiences in the right hands of a poet.

Poetry and liturgy (liturgy being the recitation of prewritten prayers alone as an individual act of worship) are also intended to be repeated, a way of making language and ideas easily remembered, a mantra that carries weight with each of its words.

Earl has often mentioned keeping his writing simple – not lacking quality, but being effective and condensing large concepts into more digestible pieces.
For example, on Tabula Rasa, saying:
“I keep it simple and dynamic
Trust the passage rites to life’s chapters
I have to write to find balance”

Poetry is Earl’s way of “keeping it brief” and passing the proverbial torch on to the listener to expand on those ideas for themselves.

The next minute: the moon is gone and you’re squinting at the glaring light of the sun, which does not return your “wink” as it blinds you.

The moon has once again abandoned you to be confronted/judged by the reality of another lost night, more lost memories and more consequences in broad daylight. In this case: Earl has realized that he smashed a girl without protection as he sobers up the next day.

line: Saw another height, had my ears poppin’
vault_lines: Saw another height, had my ears poppin'
meaning:
Earl refers to the painful effect of airplane take-offs on the eardrum, as sudden changes in atmospheric pressure (which happen when high altitudes are reached quickly) keep the air trapped in the inner ear, thus causing eardrums to push outward and “pop”.



With this metaphor, the artist could indicate either his general growth, both as a person and an artist, or the pain he suffered due to the pressure and anxiety that came with his rise in the hip-hop space while being still very young, as a member of the collective Odd Future. The latter topic was harshly tackled by Earl in his first two studio albums, Doris (2013) and I Don’t Like S–t, I Don’t Go Outside (2015), before he started settling differences with his troubled past and turned a new leaf, which was first symbolized by his 2018 LP, Some Rap Songs.

line: Out in Shoreditch
vault_lines: Focus steady and unbroken
meaning:
‘Seen Skeppy (Skepta) out in Shoreditch refers to Skepta’s (along with BBK) spontaneous highly illegal concert undertaken in a Shoreditch carpark. (Shoreditch is an area in London).

https://youtu.be/68JQmKitwZc?si=It1SmOQpDFjH4kuy

In 2010, UK Grime Artist Skepta hinted through his twitter that “I love every #Skepta supporter. One day I’m gonna have a Party in a Car Park and you can all come for free.”
Years later on April 30th 2015 at 4pm, Skepta randomly tweeted to his fans to come to a Car Park in Shoreditch at 8pm, overlooking the infamous Barbican Estate in Clerkenwell, where they would continue until the Police turn up. With no planning or permit and armed with a Red Bull sound truck, the crew celebrated Skepta’s release of his song ‘Shutdown,’ which would manifest itself as a grime classic. Skepta and BBK performed several grime tunes such as That’s Not Me and It Ain’t Safe as well as a grime set over the iconic grime instrumental Rhythm & Gash, before leading chants of ‘Fuck the Police’ and ‘BBK,’ followed by repeatedly playing Shutdown and then inevitably being shutdown by the police after about 40 minutes.



While perhaps Earl’s insertion of this lyric is also rather spontaneous, he may be reinforcing the ‘cold wind’ of the previous line, as London is notoriously frigid. Furthermore, he could be illuminating the power of social media or the legacy of pioneering music events (as this did occur in 2015, eight years after Voir Dire’s release – although this could also relate to the early recording dates of the project) as perhaps he witnessed through his ‘telly’ which leads into the next line.



(as you can see the number 8 bus to Bow Church was humourously stopped for an extended period of time).

vault_lines: He said the telly for the hoes
meaning:
In the song, the lines “He said the telly for the hoes, keep them heifers off ya doorstep” reflect a combination of streetwise advice and colloquial language that is common in hip-hop lyrics.

Here, “telly” is slang for a hotel room, while “hoes” and “heifers” are colloquial terms for women.

The advice in these lines suggests that it is better to entertain or meet women in a hotel room rather than at one’s residence, as it may help maintain privacy, boundaries, or discretion.
This advice, given by Skepta, touches on relationships and lifestyle in hip-hop culture.

These lines highlight the use of language and advice specific to the subculture of the song, emphasizing the importance of discretion and maintaining a certain image or reputation.

line: Cream creps in the cold wind
vault_lines: Cream creps in the cold wind
meaning:
The line “Cream creps in the cold wind” is a visual and sensory description that relates to fashion and weather conditions. It suggests that Earl is wearing cream-coloured sneakers or shoes, which is a fashion choice. The mention of “cold wind” indicates that it’s chilly outside, and Earl is wearing these particular shoes in those conditions.

This line highlights the contrast between fashion or style (the choice of cream-coloured shoes) and practicality (wearing them in cold weather). It shows Earl’s dedication to his fashion choices, even in less-than-ideal weather conditions. It might be a way of expressing his commitment to his style and making a statement through his appearance.

In a broader sense, it reflects the idea of self-expression and the importance of fashion and style to Earl, even when faced with adverse weather conditions. It’s a common theme in music to use fashion and style as a form of self-expression and identity.
